summary: Assigns instruction codes and defines object formats and meanings for use with the HEMS Monitoring and Control Language of RFC 1023. It is described as provisional, so definitions could change. Readers are asked to confirm with the authors that they have the latest version.

eli5.summary: It is a dictionary that says which code means which thing when asking a machine about itself, in an early network management system.

what is the hems monitoring and control language

subtitle: The dictionary of instruction codes, object formats and meanings that gave the early HEMS network-management system its vocabulary.

tldr.problem: A system for monitoring and controlling network entities needs every machine to agree on which codes mean which operations and what each readable value actually means.
tldr.mechanism: The memo assigns ASN.1 tags, external formats and meanings to the operations and to a tree of objects (dictionaries of counters, tables and settings) that an entity exposes to its query processor.
tldr.outcome: It is marked provisional: the authors expected the definitions to change and the event section in particular to need much more work.

today: The RFC states that it is provisional and that its definitions are subject to change. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its status is recorded as Unknown. It builds on the language defined in RFC 1023.

sections.title: What This Memo Defines
sections.content:
Earlier memos (RFC 1021 and RFC 1022) described the High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS), a way for applications to read and write values in remote entities that run a simple query processor. RFC 1023 defines the High-Level Monitoring and Control Language that this memo fills in.

This memo standardizes three things for every value: the ASN.1 tag assigned to it, its external representation (such as INTEGER or OCTETSTRING) and its meaning, for example which kinds of packets a particular counter really counts. The authors call the definitions provisional and ask readers to confirm they have the latest version. They assume the reader already knows ASN.1 and the IP protocol suite.
sections.eli5: This memo is the rulebook for the words used when you ask a computer about itself. It says what each word is called and what it means.

sections.title: Messages and Language Instructions
sections.content:
HEMS values travel in the data section of messages of the High-Level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP, RFC 1022). For every message type the data section is a SEQUENCE of objects: operations and operands in requests, retrieved objects in replies, and an initial event object plus related objects in events. Messages that follow this memo set the link field of the HEMP CommonHeader to 1, meaning version 1 of HEMS, and set resourceId to NULL.

Operations are sent in postfix form: operands are pushed onto a stack and the operation that follows them consumes them. To make operations easy to spot, all of them use one application-specific type, Operation, whose values include get, begin, end, get-match, get-attributes, get-attributes-match, get-range, set and set-match.
sections.eli5: You first put the things you are asking about on a pile, then say what to do with them, like laying out ingredients and then saying 'mix'.

sections.title: Design Choices Behind the Objects
sections.content:
The control language needs the objects to live in a tree-shaped type space. This memo defines one universal type space, split into required and optional portions. Implementors support the required part plus whatever optional part suits their entity, such as a gateway or a multi-user host. A special application type is reserved for vendor-specific values, which must be wrapped in a VendorSpecific object.

A stated goal is to keep processing on the entity small and put the burden of data reduction on the querying application. So the objects are mostly counters or values the entity already computes. Entities need not shrink an INTEGER to the minimum number of octets, and the heavy use of the ASN.1 SET type lets the entity return fields in whatever order is convenient.

Because several management centers may query one entity, SET must not be applied to any Counter. Changing a counter could spoil data collection by other centers. HEMS offers no protection against clashing SET requests; the authors suggest "owned" objects if that becomes necessary.
sections.eli5: The computer being asked should do as little work as possible, so the asker does the hard sums. And nobody may reset the scoreboard, because other people are reading it too.

sections.title: The Object Tree and Its Dictionaries
sections.content:
All data sits in dictionaries, each a conceptual grouping of values. The top-level RootDictionary has seven parts: SystemVariables (clocks, load, memory, up/down state), EventControls (optional, for entities that send events), Interfaces (network interfaces and IP to physical address maps), IpNetworkLayer (IP layer workings, packet counts, host traffic matrices), IpRoutingTable, IpTransportLayer (the transport protocols the entity supports) and IpApplications (optional, and left for further study).

Each object is defined with a name, an ASN.1 type, a definition, optional notes, an object status and the operations allowed on it. The status is Required, Required On Condition (needed when an optional feature such as TCP is implemented), Encouraged or Defined. The memo says it is better not to implement an object than to abuse its definition. The transport dictionary covers protocols such as ICMP, IGMP, TCP, EGP and UDP; for EGP, defined in RFC 904, the egpState values are 0 Idle, 1 Acquisition, 2 Down, 3 Up and 4 Cease.
sections.eli5: It is a filing cabinet with seven drawers, such as one for the clock, one for the network cards and one for the maps of where to send things. Each paper inside has a label saying what it means.

sections.title: Attributes, Well-Known Types and Errors
sections.content:
An application can learn what an object means by sending get-attributes, which returns an Attributes object. It always gives the ASN.1 tag (tagASN1) and the underlying type (valueFormat), and may add a long description, a short label of fewer than 15 octets, a units string, a precision and a properties bit string. Precision, the roll-over point, is required for every Counter.

The memo also defines shared types. A Counter is an unsigned integer that rolls over to 0, and its size should be chosen so it does not roll over more than once every 24 hours. A Fraction is a numerator over 256. BootClock counts milliseconds since boot, while LocalClock and NetClock count milliseconds since 00:00 1 January 1900 UTC, with 0 meaning an uninitialized clock. Others include Histogram, TrafficMatrix, IpAddress and TimeStamp.

Failures come back as an Error object with an error code, the octet offset in the query where the problem was found, and a description.
sections.eli5: Every number can come with a little tag saying what it measures and how big it can get before it starts again from zero, like a car odometer.

sections.title: Events and Open Questions
sections.content:
An event is an unsolicited message from an entity to a management center. It is formatted like a reply, but the HEMP header labels it an event and its first object is an EventLeader carrying eventCode, eventIndex, eventThreshold, eventTime and eventDescr. Required related objects follow, and more can be added through the eventExecution buffer of the matching entry. The memo lists a handful of generic events (code 1 is that the entity has rebooted) but says they are for illustration only.

The memo ends by admitting gaps: the whole event system needs thorough examination, TCP connection parameters might better be kept per connection, the round-trip-time algorithm specification needs refining, and much more research is needed on what to gather to monitor a network effectively.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the computer shouts 'I just restarted!' without being asked. The authors say the list of things worth shouting about is still a rough draft.

viz.caption: ERROR CODES IN THE ERROR OBJECT

items.label: System error
items.desc: The query processor has failed in some way.

items.label: Format error
items.desc: An error was detected in the input stream.

items.label: Stack error
items.desc: A stack overflow or underflow occurred.

items.label: Instruction error
items.desc: The instruction is unknown or not supported on that object.

items.label: Operand error
items.desc: Wrong number of operands or inappropriate operands.
